name: the Schlosspark
title: Ancient Trees in the Schlosspark, Bad Homburg: 5 to Find
meta_description: The thickest trunk here has no name, no plaque and no register entry, and it beats the famous cedars. Five trees in a park you can walk through free.
intro:
Five trees in this park are worth stopping for, and the thickest is the one nobody has named. It is a plane about ten metres east of the second wingnut, 5.66 metres round, wider than the famous cedars beside the palace. It carries no plaque and appears in no register. It turned up in a dendrologist's survey of the park in 2021 and that is the whole of its paper trail.

The cedars are the pair everyone comes for, and they earn it. Sixteen seedlings arrived from Kew through Princess Elizabeth of Great Britain, who married Landgrave Friedrich VI Joseph in 1818 and kept her English botanical contacts; two went into the ground in front of the royal wing in 1822 and both still stand there. The larger runs 6.40 metres round and 21 metres tall, and by 2011 its crown measured more than 35 metres from east to west, so the tree is considerably wider than it is high.

Two oaks of roughly the same size stand a couple of hundred metres apart, 5.39 metres at the bridge and 4.94 by the lake. Neither is dated, neither is labelled, and both are on the map because a reader sent us a Schlosspark oak of about five metres and the tip fitted either one. The fastest grower is the dawn redwood at the southern pond: about seventy years old, already 5.80 metres round and 28 metres tall, which is more girth than the cedar has managed in two centuries.

The ground has been garden since at least 1441, was laid out as a baroque garden from 1680 and remade as an English landscape park from the later eighteenth century, which is the style it still wears: grass, water, and single large trees given room. It is a Hessian state park, so walking through it costs nothing and passes no gate; the palace buildings themselves are ticketed.
